transcript:
Header
Date: 2026-03-11 14:00 UTC  Duration: ~45 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Carlos Ruiz (Redwood SE), Rachel Kim (Nimbus PM), Derek Shaw (Nimbus Eng Lead), Samir Patel (Nimbus CTO)

Summary (auto): Hosted API walkthrough focusing on chat/text generation basics -- streaming responses, key parameters (temperature, top_p, max_tokens), retry/backoff guidance, and security/hosting questions. Agreed next steps: send pricing & security docs, share benchmarks + example code, plan pilot kickoff.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Maya from Redwood. We put a quick agenda in the calendar -- quick qual, then Carlos will walk through the hosted API demo, focusing on chat and text generation, streaming, params and retry patterns, and then Q&A.
[00:12] Rachel: Thanks, Maya. Quick intro -- I'm Rachel, PM for patient messaging at Nimbus, and Derek's our eng lead. Samir's on to listen for architecture/security. We're evaluating hosted providers for a pilot.
[00:22] Derek: Hi, yeah, engineering. We mostly run on AWS EKS, using a mix of Lambda and containers. Right now we call OpenAI for NLU, but costs and latency are getting high for our use case.
[00:30] Samir: And I'm Samir. Key thing for us is PHI concerns and data residency -- we need clarity on what data leaves our VPC and retention.
[00:38] Maya: Totally. We'll cover security items and our private options briefly; Carlos will show the hosted flow and what data is retained. Any timeline or success criteria?
[00:45] Rachel: We're hoping to run a month-long pilot in April and decide by end of Q2. Success is accuracy of responses and 99th percentile latency under 600ms for short prompts.
[00:54] Maya: Great, that's helpful. Okay Carlos?
[01:00] Carlos: Cool, I'll share my screen. You should see the Redwood Console and a simple curl example. At a high level, hosted API is a REST endpoint and SDKs. We support chat and text endpoints -- chat is just a structured wrapper for multi-turn, text for single-prompt generation.
[01:20] Carlos: Here's an example request -- we set model, messages, temperature, max_tokens. For streaming we flip on stream=true and get chunked SSE responses that include partial tokens. This reduces perceived latency for UI.
[01:34] Derek: When you say streaming, is it server-sent events? Websocket?
[01:38] Carlos: By default we support SSE and SDK streaming wrappers. Websockets are possible via the SDK, but SSE covers most browser & server cases. Implementation-wise it's chunked JSON lines, each chunk has a delta.
[01:50] Rachel: Any caveats about tokenization or partial outputs being invalid JSON mid-stream?
[01:55] Carlos: Good call -- if you're using structured outputs, we recommend the function-calling / tool-calling features where the model returns a JSON blob at the end, or you can buffer tokens until the final message. Streaming may give partial non-well-formed JSON mid-stream, so client-side assembly is required.
[02:12] Maya: Also note we have structured output helpers -- you can set a schema and we run light parse validation, but it's best to post-validate.
[02:20] Carlos: Moving on to params: temperature controls randomness, top_p is nucleus sampling, max_tokens sets the cap. For deterministic completions we set temperature=0. For chat, we also have system/user roles for prompt engineering.
[02:34] Derek: Any rate limit guidance? We're expecting bursts from scheduled jobs.
[02:38] Carlos: Hosted has per-account rate limits and token quotas; those are visible in the Console. If you expect bursts we can provision burst capacity or talk about Dedicated later. Also intelligent retry is important--exponential backoff with jitter and idempotency keys for non-streaming requests.
[02:53] Rachel: How do you recommend retries for streaming?
[02:56] Carlos: For streaming, you should detect connection drop and resume at the application layer. We don't currently provide token-accurate resume for public hosted calls, so often people re-issue the request and deduplicate on the server or checkpoint partial output client-side. For pilot workloads we can discuss sticky sessions or dedicated instances.
[03:14] Derek: Do you provide SDKs in Node/Python?
[03:16] Carlos: Yes -- official SDKs for Node, Python, and a curl example. The SDKs handle streaming events and provide helpers for retries with backoff.
[03:24] Maya: I'm going to paste a sample curl in chat for the team -- shows a minimal streaming call and a non-streaming call.
[03:30] Carlos: While I paste, quick note on costs -- streaming lowers perceived latency but doesn't necessarily lower token usage; you still pay for tokens produced. We do token-based billing plus per-request overhead for some endpoints.
[03:42] Samir: On security: SOC 2, SSO, encryption at rest -- do you support KMS or HSM for customer-managed keys?
[03:48] Maya: Yes, for Private deployments we support customer-managed KMS and HSM integrations. For hosted we encrypt at rest and in transit, and we offer Bring Your Own Key for enterprise plans. We'll include the compliance pack in the follow-up.
[04:00] Samir: And audit logs?
[04:02] Carlos: Console has per-route logs and token-level cost traces. For enterprise customers we stream audit logs to your logging endpoint and include full request/response metadata (redacted on request).
[04:12] Rachel: Data residency -- can we be sure PHI doesn't leave region?
[04:15] Maya: Hosted regions are selectable; for strict residency we recommend Private (VPC) or Dedicated with region pinning. We'll capture your residency requirements as an action item.
[04:25] Derek: Back to the demo, can you show a full example with retries and idempotency?
[04:28] Carlos: Sure -- here's pseudocode. For non-streaming calls, set an idempotency token header so retries won't double-charge. For transient 5xx or rate-limit errors, implement exponential backoff with capped retries. For 429 specifically, respect Retry-After when present.
[04:43] Carlos: Also show quick benchmark -- on our hosted tier, typical p50 latency for short prompts is ~120-250ms depending on model; p95 depends more on sequence length. For Nimbus's latency target (600ms p99) this is achievable for short prompts on hosted, but if you need strict SLOs we'd recommend Dedicated.
[04:58] Samir: Those numbers -- are they for unlocked tokens or with KV cache?
[05:02] Carlos: Those are for typical workloads with prefix caching enabled. If you have heavy context reuse, caching reduces compute and latency.
[05:10] Rachel: How do you handle context windows and long conversations?
[05:13] Carlos: We support long context models and streaming for that. We also provide KV cache and assisted chunking in the SDK. For extremely long histories we recommend summarization + retrieval to keep tokens manageable.
[05:26] Derek: Any gotchas for EKS-based clients calling hosted endpoints?
[05:29] Carlos: Nothing special -- most customers run a small gateway in their VPC to manage keys and rate-limit. We also provide signed tokens and short-lived credentials for servers.
[05:38] Maya: I'm going to switch to Console view -- show API keys, usage dashboard, per-route latency, model catalog. Carlos can demo how to pin a model and view a benchmark.
[05:50] Carlos: Here we have model profiles -- each model shows throughput, token cost, and recommended quantization. For experiments, you can create a route, pin a model, and set rollout policies -- canary, A/B, fallback to cheaper variant.
[06:04] Rachel: That fallback sounds useful -- so if capacity is constrained it will route to a compatible variant automatically?
[06:08] Carlos: Exactly -- smart routing rules: by latency, cost, region, or tier. We can configure automatic fallback when a model is overloaded.
[06:16] Derek: One more -- how do you test quality regressions?
[06:19] Carlos: We have Redwood Optimize -- you can tie prompt sets and evals to a route. On deploy, you can run eval suites and get regression alerts. That would help during pilot to track accuracy changes.
[06:30] Rachel: Great. Are there sample prompts or an eval harness you can share?
[06:33] Carlos: Yes -- I'll share a lightweight eval harness and a benchmark CSV. Maya will include links in the follow-up.
[06:40] Samir: About pricing -- ballpark for hosted pilots?
[06:44] Maya: For pilots we typically offer usage-based pricing with an introductory credit; we'll send a pilot pricing template. If you need reserved capacity later, we can discuss Dedicated pricing.
[06:52] Derek: Any pitfalls we should watch for when switching from OpenAI to Redwood API?
[06:56] Carlos: Mostly prompt tuning and model differences -- tokens and outputs vary slightly. We recommend ab testing a subset of prompts and using the eval tool to identify regressions. Also update any rate-limit handling to account for per-account quotas.
[07:10] Rachel: Ok let's recap next steps.
[07:12] Maya: Recap: Maya will send pricing and the security pack (SOC2/ISO + KMS details). Carlos will send benchmark CSV, sample curl and SDK streaming snippets, and the eval harness. Nimbus will confirm residency and pilot scope. We'll tentatively schedule pilot kickoff week of 2026-03-22.
[07:30] Derek: Sounds good. One last technical Q -- for long running streaming requests is there a max connection time?
[07:34] Carlos: There's a connection timeout on the hosted gateway around 120s by default; for very long-running streams we recommend chunking or using a dedicated session in Dedicated that supports longer durations.
[07:45] Samir: Thanks everyone -- useful session.
[07:47] Maya: Thanks all -- we'll follow up via email with the artifacts.
[07:50] Rachel: Thanks, bye.

Notes: occasional transcription artifacts (Redwood heard as RedWord in one clip), some technical terms abbreviated (KV cache as CV cache in auto transcript). Links shared during call: [Pricing deck link], [Security pack link], [Benchmark CSV], [Sample curl + SDK snippets].
